The genuine link at this verse is to Acts 9:2, on a shorter run with a matching situation.

reason: Six words of geography, proposed again at 28:5. 'Go up to the land of Nephi' is the fixed Book of Mormon expression for this journey and occurs many times in Mosiah; Ezekiel 38:11's Gog going up to the land of unwalled villages has no other contact.

The third appearance in this batch of a mis-ranked candidate on this phrase; see the entries at Mosiah 27:14 and 27:36. Note that Mosiah 28:2 does not in fact read 'knowledge of the truth' but 'the knowledge of the Lord their God', so the run is shorter than the ranking implies.

'The LORD their God' is among the KJV's commonest divine designations and Mosiah 28:2 uses it three times in one verse. Also proposed here from 2 Kings 17:14 and Exodus 29:46 on the same run; the last of these was excluded at Mosiah 26:26 for the same reason.

Genuinely tempting, and worth the entry for the thread it seems to belong to. 'Vilest' occurs in exactly one KJV verse in this sense, Psalm 12:8, 'when the vilest men are exalted' — and Psalm 12 is also the KJV's flattery psalm, 'with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak', which would tie 28:4 back to the flattering words of Mosiah 26:6 and the 'much flattery' of 27:8. The thread does not hold. Psalm 12:8's vilest men are the wicked in power, and Mosiah 28:4's are penitents describing what they used to be; the superlative is one any writer forms from an ordinary adjective; and 26:6's 'flattering words' is a KJV singleton belonging to 1 Thessalonians 2:5, not to Psalm 12's 'flattering lips', which is a different noun. Recorded because a reader tracing the flattery vocabulary across these three chapters would very reasonably arrive here.

A five-word run that straddles a clause boundary in both texts: John 6:54's 'hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day' against Mosiah's 'they shall have eternal life; and I will deliver thy sons'. The shared words are the noun phrase plus a connective and a pronoun. The Johannine link at this verse is to John 17:20, on the believing-through-another's-word idiom.

Worth considering because Galatians 1:13 is an established source in this batch — it stands behind Mosiah 27:10 and, with 1:14, behind Mosiah 26:1 — so a third contact would be a real pattern rather than a coincidence. It is not one. 'Beyond measure' occurs in three KJV verses, two of them in Mark of crowds astonished at a miracle, and it is an ordinary intensifier in all three. Mosiah 28:12's 'desirous beyond measure, to know concerning those people which had been destroyed' is a curiosity, and Galatians 1:13's is a persecution. Nothing but the intensifier is shared.

Ranked at 28:13 by the machine but the run belongs at 28:17. Acts 11:19's 'they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen' uses 'upon' causally — scattered because of the persecution — and Mosiah 28:17 uses it spatially, scattered upon the face of the earth. The preposition is doing opposite work in the two verses, and the completing phrase is Genesis 11:9's, where the link is filed.
